newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fire-hit Channel tunnel reopens for passenger cars.
newsitem.headline: Fire-hit Channel tunnel reopens for passenger cars.

text.p: Passenger car shuttle services resumed through the Anglo-French Channel tunnel on Tuesday, three weeks after a fire closed the undersea rail link.

The first Le Shuttle train, carrying 61 vehicles, left the Coquelles terminal near Calais at 7:30 a.m. (0630 GMT) and arrived at the Cheriton terminal in southeastern England 50 minutes later, about 15 minutes longer than the journey time before the accident because of damage in the twin-bore tunnel.

The 50 km (30 mile) long tunnel was closed to all traffic on November 18, when a fire on a truck destroyed a freight vehicle shuttle train and severely damaged a section of the tunnel. Thirty-four people were injured.
Rail service for passengers between Paris and London and Brussels and London resumed last Wednesday. No date has been set for a resumption of the shuttle service for trucks.

Passengers boarding Tuesday's first car train brushed aside safety concerns after the fire and a bomb on a Paris city train by suspected Algerian Moslem militants last week that killed four people and injured more than 90.

"I don't see why we should be frightened," said Bruno, a trader in charcoal who lives in Lille in northern France and works in London. "When a plane crashes or when two trains collide, it doesn't stop other planes or trains from leaving."
"The Shuttle is faster than other means of transport across the Channel and it's more reliable in terms of timetables," he added.
"We'll see what happens, but we're confident," said a Belgian couple off to buy Christmas presents in London.
"The tunnel is one of those places where there is never a zero risk," shrugged another French traveller.
The crossings for car passengers using Le Shuttle will be from five to 15 minutes longer than normal.
And, until December 19, the service will run at 50 percent of its rate before the accident with one leaving in each direction every 40 minutes, a Eurotunnel spokesman said.
The train slowed down twice during the crossing to move from one of the parallel rail tunnels to the other one. One of the tunnels is still undergoing repairs and only two-thirds of it can be used.

The reopening of the passenger car service was welcomed by shopkeepers who rely heavily on people using the trains. The turnover of a shopping precinct located near the Calais terminal has dropped by some 30 per cent in the last three weeks.
